item.title: How Curiosity and Preparing Well Can Bring Peace in Divorce
item.description:
Divorce

How Curiosity and Preparing Well Can Bring Peace in Divorce

Jacinta Gallant on why listening to understand helps families of gray divorce

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • An adversarial process can harm parents and children. Most families do not need court.
  • Listening with curiosity before giving advice helps people feel grounded and reach their own insights.
  • Being prepared in a safe learning environment opens the mind to more possibilities during and after divorce.

This article is the second in a series that provides practical takeaways from three pioneers in family conflict resolution, who, through their decades of experience, have become internationally respected peacemakers and trainers of families and divorce professionals. Click here to read the first article.

Families of gray divorce, which refers to couples 50 and older, often become mired in conflict and struggle with effective communication. Family members can feel pulled to align with a parent or sibling. Not being able to listen to understand each other can lead to emotional outbursts, pain, anger, fights, and becoming estranged.

In recognition of Conflict Resolution Day, which is observed internationally on the third Thursday of October every year, and of the approaching holiday season that promotes giving thanks and peace throughout the world, I spoke with Jacinta Gallant, Canadian family lawyer, mediator, conflict educator, and international trainer.

Source: RDNE / Pexels

A former client stopped Jacinta in a grocery store with words that show why her approach works. I’ll share them later in the interview.

Carol Hughes: Looking back over your career, what experiences or realizations led you to believe there was a better way for families to resolve the conflicts of divorce?

Jacinta Gallant: As a lawyer advocate, I had my share of “wins” and “losses,” but soon realized that most families lost in an adversarial justice system. I decided I could no longer use my talent to make things worse, so I became a mediator. In this role, I got to know both “sides” and was able to explore what each family needed for healthy coparenting and better outcomes for children.

This was a pivotal change for my career. I felt far more satisfied, even joyful, in my work. The missing piece arrived with the development of interdisciplinary collaborative practice, which brings together lawyers and mental health professionals to truly meet the needs of each family. Many lawyers are not natural “team” players, but I am—and I find it so rewarding working with other disciplines in a shared mission to support healthy families and communities.

CH: You have studied conflict resolution for decades. What are the important points that family members need to understand about what conflict is and how to resolve it?

JG: I wish the public knew that their choice of lawyer and the approach they take will have a profound impact on their family for a very long time. There are rare occasions when parents or children need the protection of family court. But almost all families don’t. Most parents don’t realize the harm that will come to their family in an adversarial court proceeding, and soon after they decide to separate, they “lawyer up.” I hate that term!

The “family justice” system is built on an adversarial model that applies facts to law and is ill-suited to managing relational dynamics and meeting children’s needs. The best family lawyers will say that therapeutic support is more important than anything else in the early stage of separation. They will acknowledge that it is almost impossible to provide firm and relevant initial advice because more information is needed. Despite this, traditional family lawyers often revert to advocating and focus on protecting their own client. That “zealous advocacy” can ignore the deeper needs of the whole family—especially the children.

CH: At some point, you chose to extend your work beyond helping individual families to writing, teaching, and training other professionals. What inspired you to broaden your reach, and what did you hope would change as a result?

JG: Most family lawyers and judges really care. I thought if I could help train more lawyers in conflict resolution, the families and their communities would benefit. I took time out in 2018 to study the insight approach to conflict, and it changed everything for me. Bringing this to the legal and mental health community has been the most rewarding aspect of my career. Drs. Cheryl Picard and Kenneth Melchin explain the distinguishing features of the insight approach in a paper listed in the references below.

CH: After all you have witnessed and learned over the course of your career, what gives you hope about the future of how families experience and resolve divorce conflict?

JG: I met a client in the grocery store last week, and she said, “It’s happening! You said we would meet someday in the future, and I would be OK. And I am.”

She gave me a hug and was so full of appreciation. What did I do that made the difference? I listened and demonstrated a sincere desire to understand her before giving her any “advice.” I dropped my “know-it-all” mentality (an occupational hazard for lawyers) and harnessed the power of curiosity. My curiosity grounded us both and led to insights.

My clients leave our office feeling better than when they walked in. I now conduct my initial client consultations with more listening, less telling. This leads to better communication and better outcomes.

CH: Your Our Family in Two Homes and Our Family in a Few Homes workbooks emphasize helping families prepare before they begin creating solutions. What have you learned about how preparation shapes families’ experience and resolution of divorce conflict?

JG: In 2019, I asked my clients what it was like to work with me. I wanted to improve their experience. They thought I asked great questions, and they often had better answers after they left my office. They appreciated our deeper (non-law) conversations but often worried about how much it was costing them. And they said they wish they had been better prepared for each stage of our work together.

So, I poured their generous feedback and my emerging understanding of the insight approach to conflict into creating client preparation tools that are now being used with families around the world. The resources are intentionally curious—meant to elicit the client’s own discoveries about themselves at a time when most people are so stressed they have no curiosity!

The preparation engages them in a safe learning experience that opens their minds to more possibilities. They engage in self-reflection without resistance because they can do this on their own time and on their own dime. With this preparation, when they meet with their chosen divorce professional, they feel more grounded and ready to engage. We have had such a positive response that we have created a public version so that every family can access the resources, often before they call a lawyer. Choose a collaborative lawyer or mediator.

item.title: Can a Mental Health Crisis Ever Be a Gift?
item.description:
Bipolar Disorder

Can a Mental Health Crisis Ever Be a Gift?

A breakdown can be a breakthrough, but the illness deserves no credit.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • A crisis can lead to positive change without having been designed for it; the meaning comes afterward.
  • We construct meaning from mental illness with family who keep showing up and from clinicians who listen.
  • Redemption stories carry a survivorship bias, and many people with serious mental illness never get one.
Source: Egor Yakushkin/Unsplash

Two years ago, I found myself locked in a county jail for four months because of threats I made while in a manic psychosis. I had spent almost a decade eluding treatment for my bipolar I disorder, and the consequences of that circumvention had caught up with me. Behind bars for the first time in my life, and surrounded by beige concrete, I took cold comfort in Nietzsche’s concept of amor fati, or love of one’s fate. Instead of accepting my fate, I thought of counterfactuals: What if I had accepted my diagnosis earlier? What if I had gone to the hospital instead of insisting I was fine?

Two years later, I find peace in a routine of stability and sobriety and writing and advocacy. I have a treatment plan that works for me, have rekindled a loving relationship with my mother after 10 years of estrangement, and have embarked on a career of mental health advocacy that grew out of the wreckage of a catastrophe.

Now, the impulse to tell a redemptive story is tempting. It would be easy, compelling, and even flattering to say that the illness was the price I had to pay for everything good that followed. A reckoning with the past invites the tantalizing questions: Can a mental health crisis be a gift? Who gets to decide?

In an essay from earlier this year, psychiatrist Awais Aftab narrates two recent accounts: although Tyler Alterman could not get out of bed for over a year, he now says that he is grateful for the depression that saved his life; Jazmine Russell considers her psychotic episode an inspiring lesson in how her life was once breaking her down. These narratives have real therapeutic value, since they translate the senseless suffering of psychic collapse into a language that one can speak confidently into the future.

I know their appeal. The remorse I feel, the memoir I’m writing, the advocacy talks I give—none of it could have come without the calamity that came before. Psychologists call this kind of change post-traumatic growth, and research suggests it is common.

Why Mental Illness Is Not an Adaptation

It feels seductive to see mental health disorders as a type of evolutionary adaptation that confers advantages on a suffering soul. But as evolutionary psychiatrist Randolph Nesse points out, this is a fallacy. Low mood and anxiety may be useful defenses, but “diseases are not adaptations shaped by natural selection.” As Aftab explains, a symptom (such as a loss of sleep) can lead to positive changes in one’s life (such as improved sleep hygiene) without having been designed for it. A death of a loved one may alter the course of one’s life for the better, encouraging one to cherish remaining relationships, but no one with a straight face would call that death a gift.

In my case, I would be hard-pressed to find the good in my mania. While it felt like clarity, like the best version of me I had ever embodied, it made me cruel and selfish, and it cleared my life of family and friends.

While in jail and during my 10 months at a state psychiatric hospital, I tried to find meaning in my chaos. Whereas I once thought, I am a failure, I learned to reframe the global indictment into the more contained expression of I had failed. The failure supplied the raw material to craft something new. I took solace in Viktor Frankl’s expression of “the last of the human freedoms—to choose one’s attitude.” Edith Eger inspired me with her idea that “the opposite of depression is expression.”

Still, meaning-making was hardly a solitary act: my mother kept showing up to visit me, and read books on bipolar disorder and neuroscience alongside me; at the hospital, I met weekly with a caring psychologist who asked me about how I processed my shame. To call my illness and the decade of destruction it wrought a gift would be to credit it with my mother’s persistence and my psychologist’s curiosity, along with the arduous work I did myself.

Source: Colby Winfield/Unsplash

Who Gets Left Out of Redemption Stories

But as I learned from my stay at that state hospital, not everyone has cognitive access to Frankl’s freedoms. My neighbor, whom I will call Johnnie, had spent decades at the institution, where he battled voices for what seemed like every hour of every day. He often interjected during our therapeutic groups with quirky one-liners. Rain tastes like Southern Comfort and moonshine. And that’s dangerous. Or I’m Johnnie, and today is a miracle, even with the rain.

Psychologist Steven Heine notes that intense trauma “can completely upend people’s meaning frameworks,” leaving some to “struggle, sometimes for decades.” The allure of a redemptive narrative is that it is written by a survivor, and hidden behind that appeal is a kind of survivorship bias. The very process of looking back on a past crisis, as Aftab says, distorts our perception of the crisis. While a crisis may be one route to change, it is rarely the best one. Telling someone in the middle of a psychotic episode, or a father waiting in an emergency room lobby, that their pain may turn out to be a gift risks romanticizing an episode, forcing a search on demand to find meaning in catastrophe.

Aftab provides a similar lesson for clinicians when he suggests that psychiatrists “should honor the patient’s meaning-making while being mindful of its fallibility.” For every person who can trumpet how a crisis saved their life, far too many, like Johnnie, are prisoners to illnesses that have given them nothing.

While I was initially drawn to the bravado of amor fati, I remained attached to it over time because it taught me the discipline of gratitude. I had the drive, determination, and education to make sense of a crippling mental illness whose riddle the mental health system seemed uninterested in helping me solve. I recovered because I read deeply about the illness that almost took my life, but I also recovered because I never felt alone: I had a mother who kept my memory alive for a decade, and who kept showing up for me because she believed in the promise of her son.

The redemptive arc—the notion that a mental health breakdown can be a breakthrough—is appealing to our quick-fix culture. But it is better to be honest: I can accept all the ugly that has happened, and even love the life it led to, without needing to claim that the illness taught me a necessary lesson in life.

item.title: When Setting Boundaries Backfires
item.description:
Boundaries

When Setting Boundaries Backfires

Finally saying no can be a lot messier than we might be hoping.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Setting boundaries can be an important step towards protecting yourself from burnout.
  • Bowen's family systems theory explains why changing how you behave in your family system can lead to backlash.
  • Setting boundaries can be a lot harder than you had expected, and it is OK to ask for help when you're stuck.
Source: PixelsEffect / iStock

Lisa was at the end of her tether. The demands of her life had started to weigh on her so heavily that she felt crushed under the burden of it all. Lisa came to me because she had difficulty getting out of bed in the morning; she felt numb, flat, and low most days, and nothing in her life gave her joy anymore.

She had three kids and had, through sheer grit and self-abandonment, built a successful business that allowed her to work from home, while her husband worked a highly demanding city job. She was responsible for all her kids’ activities, school runs, the house, and everything that came with it. When her mother became ill, and Lisa had to add regular hospital visits to her to-do list, something in her broke. She was done.

Recognizing needs

Lisa was suffering from burnout. She had been raised to be the “good daughter,” “good mother,” and “good wife,” and any departure from those self-assigned roles felt like a betrayal to the life she had built. In therapy, we started to work on Lisa just noticing her own feelings and needs, but it was difficult for her to stay with herself. Any stretch she made to step out of one of her roles, an all-mighty guilt force would pull her back in. If she looked after herself, her kids might suffer, her mum might be alone, her husband might feel more overwhelmed. Lisa felt stuck, and she was.

She got there in the end, but only because the alternative now felt untenable. She had been barely sleeping for months, and her body was under constant tension that she couldn’t switch off from anymore. She let go of bits of her to-do list; she asked her sister to check in on her mum and her husband to drop the kids off a few days a week. She started to create boundaries around her own capacity and communicated them to the family system around her. She felt elated. But neither of us was fully prepared for what happened next.

Systems don’t like change

When Lisa’s husband realized that she was asking for permanent changes to their daily routine, he started picking fights, accusing her of being selfish and putting too much pressure on him. He invalidated her feelings and reminded her how much time off she had compared to him. Lisa’s children rebelled, and her sister became distant and stopped taking Lisa’s calls.

Lisa was devastated and felt completely unseen. She was stuck between her new and old self, unable to move forward in either direction. What was happening to her family? Why could they not understand what she was going through?

Families, according to Bowen’s family system theory, are deeply interconnected. If one person changes, the whole system has to change. Lisa setting boundaries for the first time triggered her family to push back because the easiest way for the whole system to regain equilibrium would be for Lisa to return to her overfunctioning self.

Lisa’s systems had grown around the role she had been playing in them. She had taken on most of the childcare responsibilities, and her husband’s and her children’s expectations were built around that. With Lisa playing her part, the system was in balance, seemingly. When Lisa changed the rules, the system tumbled out of kilter.

Bowen suggested that differentiation of the self in an emotionally interconnected system goes through several stages—the act of setting the boundary, the system pushing back, and the boundary having to be maintained in the face of that pushback so that the system can adapt. Bowen essentially postulated that, in a system under high pressure or anxiety, you cannot expect boundary setting to go smoothly. Pushback is a predictable step in achieving differentiation and also what makes “saying no” so unbelievably hard.

The next step

Most of Lisa’s therapy sessions from that point forward revolved around understanding whether Lisa wanted to continue in her marriage. Lisa’s guilt had kept her going for years. It had protected her from the very real possibility of a huge relational rupture with her partner and her family. But now, if her husband couldn’t see how much she was suffering, how could she be with him?

Bowen’s theory clues us in as to why change in Lisa’s family was so difficult, and it also reminds us that things are rarely as black and white as they seem at first glance. Lisa was self-employed, and setting boundaries for her had less impact on her job but saved her from burnout. Her husband’s boss, however, noticed him being late a few mornings and had a chat with him about his commitment to his role. Lisa’s husband suddenly felt helpless, and his anxiety became overwhelming. He blamed Lisa without thinking and pushed her further away.

Reevaluating relationships

When Lisa changed the rules, she and her husband had to re-evaluate their lives in fundamental ways. Lisa’s husband had been working in a job he hated for years because of the financial obligations of having three children. When Lisa and her husband were honest with each other, they realized that Lisa’s burnout had brought to light fissures in their family system that had been there for a long time. It took a lot of effort and honesty for them to rebuild a life that took both of their needs into account.

Other times, relationships will fall apart when one person steps out of their assigned role, and we have to be honest about how interconnected and dependent on each other we are as human beings. Boundary setting is not always as easy as our quick-fix culture would like us to believe. Saying no when your guilt has been keeping you overfunctioning for decades is empowering and freeing, but it will likely mean altering the relationships in your life, sometimes drastically.

If you are finding it hard to set boundaries, remind yourself that this is not meant to be easy. Seek professional help and always take small steps to give the systems around you and yourself a chance to adapt. True change is hard; don’t try to do it on your own.

item.title: Journaling Can Get Anxiety Out of Your Head
item.description:
Anxiety

Journaling Can Get Anxiety Out of Your Head

You can quiet the noise in your head by putting thoughts on paper.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Journaling provides a simple, effective way to get worries out of your head.
  • Putting pen to paper encourages self-reflection.
  • You don't need perfect words or a lengthy entry to feel more grounded.

Sometimes the mind won’t stop looping and replaying. Anxiety has a way of showing up at the most inconvenient times. You're at a birthday party, hanging out with friends, sitting in class, trying to finish homework, or even lying in bed trying to fall asleep. Suddenly, there’s that thought or stream of thoughts. The “What Ifs.” "What if something goes wrong?” The constant stream of negative thoughts runs through your head, and there is no ‘stop’ button

In my work with people of all ages, I see how easily anxious thoughts can hijack our attention. They interrupt our ability to be present, interfere with concentration, and sometimes make even the simplest tasks feel overwhelming. The problem isn't always the thought itself. It's what happens when we get stuck in the cycle of thinking, rethinking, analyzing, and overanalyzing. What do we do with all of that mental noise? Sometimes, the answer is surprisingly simple: Put it on paper.

There's Something Powerful About Putting Pen to Paper

Writing out our thoughts can be therapeutic, but we don't always need an audience. We live in a world where just about everything happens on a screen. We text, scroll, type, swipe, and communicate in abbreviations. Somewhere along the way, we seem to have lost the art of slowing down and writing by hand with pen and paper rather than texting or typing on a keyboard.

Journaling is more than writing down what happened during your day. It's an opportunity to slow your brain down long enough to process what's happening inside of it. The neuropsychological component of writing: When we journal, we're engaging multiple areas of our brain. We have to organize our thoughts, retrieve information, put feelings into words, sequence our ideas, and translate them into written language.

We're also engaging executive functioning skills, including working memory, organization, planning, and self-monitoring. There’s an emotional component. Sometimes we don't even realize how we're feeling until we start writing. A thought that seemed so big in our heads might look a little different once it's on paper. We may begin to recognize patterns, identify triggers, or realize that what we're worried about isn't necessarily what we're upset about. Writing allows us to pause, reflect, and look at our thoughts from a different perspective. It's not about having perfect handwriting, perfect grammar, or writing something profound. It's about permitting yourself to be honest.

Your Brain Needs a Break

We can remind ourselves, especially as parents, that we spend so much time filling our days. Our children's days are filled with school, homework, sports, activities, social commitments, and screens. Our own days are filled with work, responsibilities, errands, family obligations, and the never-ending to-do list. We're constantly moving from one thing to the next. But when do we stop? When do we give ourselves (and our children) the chance to slow down, reflect, and reconnect?

We talk a lot about helping children develop emotional regulation skills, but we forget children need opportunities to practice identifying and expressing what they're feeling. Journaling can be one of those opportunities. For younger children, it might mean drawing a picture, writing a few words, or having a parent help them put their feelings into sentences. For adolescents, it might be a private notebook where they can work through friendships, school stress, social pressures, and all those complicated feelings that come with growing up.

Just Get Started

If you or your child aren't sure what to write, try starting with one of these:

  • What am I worried about right now?
  • What is something I wish I could say but haven't?
  • What is within my control, and what isn't?
  • What would I tell a friend who was feeling this way?
  • What went well today?
  • What do I need right now?

Reconnect With Yourself

Journaling isn't a magic cure for anxiety, and it doesn't mean that every worry will disappear once you put it on paper. But it can help create some distance between you and your thoughts. It can help you recognize patterns, process emotions, organize your thinking, and feel a little more in control. Most importantly, it gives you something we don't make enough time for anymore: uninterrupted time with yourself. So, put down the phone. Close the laptop. Grab a notebook and a pen.

You don't need to write a novel, sound intelligent, or even make sense. Just start writing because sometimes the best way to quiet the noise in your head is to give those thoughts somewhere else to go.

item.title: Innovators at Work: The Price for Breaking the Rules
item.description:
Creativity

Innovators at Work: The Price for Breaking the Rules

What roadblocks do innovators face at work, and what do they need from leaders?

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Ethically disruptive innovators identify and solve problems through prosocial and creative means.
  • Innovators are often punished for bucking the status quo and breaking group norms.
  • Leaders' characteristics and sense of self impact how they react to innovators.
  • The best leaders engage in innovative work instead of simply facilitating the creative processes of others.

Ethical disruptive innovators identify and solve problems through prosocial and creative means that often unsettle group norms.

Disruption can be interpreted both as destructive and divine, depending on the professional culture. For example, part-time Sherwin-Williams employee Tony Piloseno, a senior at the time at Ohio University, used his popular TikTok channel to share his paint-mixing acumen, a clever contribution meant to bolster the company’s products, yet instead of accolades, he was served termination papers for violating company policy. However, instead of accepting one of the multiple job offers spurred by the news coverage, he poured his energy into starting his own paint company, a bold innovator’s move (Tonester Paints, n.d.).

Deciphering the Cultural Norms at Work

Organizational norms govern how employees typically behave at work, but norms can be messy business, for institutions possess multiple forms. There are injunctive norms, which are the “ought to” behaviors, and descriptive norms, which detail what people actually do. When a gap exists between the two, the Focus Theory of Normative Conduct suggests we follow the norms we see others live out (Cialdini et al., 1991).

For example, let’s say that during faculty meetings, university administrators regularly profess that they value employee well-being (injunctive norms), yet faculty workload dictates 70-hour work weeks, and the university gym is free to students, but not to employees. Faculty will work longer hours and exercise fewer hours, putting their health at risk, because the descriptive norm is what plays out on campus despite injunctive norms to the contrary (Cialdini et al., 1990; Roswag et al., 2026; Skogstad et al., 2017).

Characteristics of Ethical Disruptive Innovators

We are shaped by those with whom we share our social spaces, so what happens when an employee decides to think past tradition, explore new ideas, and forge unique connections in a quest to innovate novel solutions to organizational problems (Lawande, 2023)?

Dyer and colleagues (2011) studied just that, interviewing creators of groundbreaking products and founders and leaders of visionary companies. They shared their insights in the book The Innovator’s DNA: Mastering the Five Skills of Disruptive Innovators. Across their interviews, surveys, and research, five characteristics bubbled up from their data, finding that innovators passionately practice:

  1. Associating: seeking connections amongst disparate questions, thoughts, and ideas and across diverse disciplines and industries.
  2. Questioning: asking why, why not, and what if? They challenge conventional wisdom and approaches in an effort to bust past the status quo.
  3. Observing: closely examining the active and passive behaviors of diverse groups pertinent to the puzzle to be solved; adopting the lens of an anthropologist conducting fieldwork.
  4. Networking: connecting with and learning from individuals with divergent expertise and cultural backgrounds.
  5. Experimenting: seeking novel experiences to stretch their perspectives, trying out unique solutions to knotty problems, and continuously iterating new prototypes based on incoming information.

Another intriguing finding was that, though many companies’ leaders facilitated processes that encouraged innovation, they themselves did not engage in innovative work. Conversely, in highly innovative organizations, making up just 15 percent of Dyer et al.’s (2009) research, top executives were among the ones actually doing, not delegating, innovation. Therefore, the injunctive (ought to) and descriptive (actually doing) organizational norms were in alignment, thus providing a clear pathway for others to join in or initiate creative work.

Again, we tend to emulate what we see, and leaders set that agenda. But what happens to innovative employees in organizations where leadership views their innovator’s DNA as a threat, not an asset?

The Diverse Ways Leaders Respond to Innovation

Ethical disruption awakens innovation, but as Tony experienced, shaking trees has its costs; keepers of the status quo sometimes go to considerable lengths to neutralize norm-breakers. Norm violations are categorized as either constructive, such as crafting innovative products that surpass current offerings, or destructive, like purposefully denigrating a colleague’s reputation. The disruptor’s intentions and the innovation’s success also factor into how the norm is classified (Bennett et al., 2024). Though organizations often profess a desire for “out-of-the-box” thinkers, many nonconformists face roadblocks and repercussions. Whether the disruptor receives praise or pushback is, in large part, reflective of leadership.

According to McGregor’s (1960) seminal book, The Human Side of Enterprise, leaders adopt one of two theories when developing their style of management. Leaders with a Theory X view of management assume employees are lazy and shirk responsibility; therefore, they must be micromanaged, leaving little room for innovation. In contrast, leaders who view management through a Theory Y framework believe work can be fun, employees are internally motivated to do a good job, and that when given autonomy and resources, they can and will engage in creative work. Thus, under Theory Y leadership, innovators innovate.

Another way to think about leadership approaches that stymie innovation is through what researchers call control appraisal. Leaders with a low control appraisal struggle with self-doubt and believe they have limited ability to control outcomes. This group is unsettled by innovators, viewing them as unpredictable and destabilizing. Thus, they are quick to shut them down, often using withdrawal of opportunities and ostracization as containment strategies. By contrast, leaders with high control appraisal are self-confident and possess a strong sense of personal agency, or trust that they have the skills and fortitude to impact outcomes. These leaders are intrigued by innovators and work to form genuine connections, believing disruptors’ creativity is an asset, thus supporting and celebrating their work (Peng et al., 2026).

Social comparison theory is another helpful tool for considering leaders’ level of support for ethical disruptive innovators. It posits that leaders with a low core self-evaluation, or a propensity to question their ability to steer the ship, often become jealous of employees who exhibit high leadership potential (HLP), worried their star might surpass their own, and thus attempt to eliminate the competition by withdrawing opportunities. Conversely, comparison is minimal to nonexistent in leaders with a high core self-evaluation, and this positioning calls them to support innovative projects and proposals with the potential to bolster the institution’s success and more effectively serve communities (Yu et al., 2025).

Lastly, when faced with ethically disruptive innovators who don’t conform to the prevailing work culture, knowingly or unknowingly breaking group norms, leaders tend to react in one of five ways: forgive, reward, punish, ignore, or manipulate. According to research, however, only the reward reaction ensures the creative continues to engage in innovative behaviors. So, when a leader shuts down an innovator, the employee and the organization both lose out (Lin et al., 2016).

What Innovators Need From Leadership

So, what does this all tell us about the types of leaders innovators need to engage in trailblazing work? First, innovators need leaders who clearly articulate and live into their mission, ensuring their injunctive norms (ought tos) and descriptive norms (what people actually do) are in alignment. Second, innovators benefit from leaders who build authentic relationships with their employees, not just rule-followers in their inner circle. Third, innovators thrive when working for leaders who personally engage in innovative work, and by that example, the institution develops a collective culture of creativity and care.

item.title: Can Creativity Make You Happier?
item.description:
Creativity

Can Creativity Make You Happier?

Creativity can improve well-being, happiness, and health.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Creative pursuits can lower stress and improve mood.
  • Social connections can deepen with shared creative activity.
  • Anyone can learn to be more creative with practice.
Source: Photo by Jennie Razumnaya on Unsplash

The game show Family Feud pits two families against each other in a race to find the most popular answers to silly questions like “Name something you might find in a bathtub.” If you guessed “water” and 50 of the 100 people who had been surveyed had also chosen that answer, you would get those points. If you answered “arachnid,” you might get zero points. Even though many children learned the "Itsy-Bitsy Spider" song growing up, "arachnid" would probably not be one of the most-popular answers.

Creative, unconventional, divergent thinkers might be at a disadvantage on Family Feud. Yet research demonstrates that generating creative, original thought and activity can make you happier (Tan, et al. 2021).

Stress and Creativity

Moderate stress, like what you might feel when taking a test, can improve our convergent thinking—the type of thinking that's required when we want to find the right answer to a question or a problem. However, stress can stifle divergent, out-of-the-box, creative problem-solving. Divergent thinking involves generating multiple novel ideas from multiple perspectives and/or combinations of perspectives (Guo et al., 2024). When we feel looser, freer, and more relaxed, we can access our creative mind more readily.

Creativity can lower stress by offering outlets for strong emotions. Poets, authors, songwriters, dancers, and other artists find that strong emotions can fuel creativity as they strive to transform pain into beauty. Psychotherapists often recommend creative writing, journaling, and other artistic outlets as a therapeutic intervention. Creativity can increase well-being, providing opportunities to feel more fully alive and joyful (Tan, et al. 2021).

Social Connection and Creativity

Every month, a group of friends gathers at our home for a musical jam session. We improvise songs, switch instruments, and often end by drumming on percussion instruments. This shared creativity strengthens our friendship and our sense of playfulness. Engaging in creative arts with others reduces loneliness and supports social connection, an essential requirement for happiness (Perkins, et al. 2021).

Many young people have formed deep friendships from Dungeons and Dragons, Magic: The Gathering, and similar role-playing games that require creative imagination, divergent thinking, and sometimes even elaborate costume creations.

Studies show that group-based arts and creativity programs can improve the health, well-being, and quality of life of older people. These activities strengthen social ties, encourage an active imagination, and promote physical activity, all essential for a healthy life (Sowerby, et al. 2026).

“But I’m Not Creative”

When I suggest to clients that they might improve their happiness by finding a creative outlet, I often hear, “But I’m not a creative person.” I usually ask them a few questions like, “Have you ever substituted a different ingredient in a recipe when you didn’t have the right ingredients? Or have you ever had to try different ways to teach your child how to tie shoelaces?” Typically, people can think of several times in the recent past when they have been creative.

Author, psychotherapist, and writing coach Marni Freedman writes in her delightful new book, Artistic Badassery, “The latest research on creativity from both a psychological and a neuroscientific perspective shows that creativity is not an inborn gift or a fixed trait, but rather a set of skills that can be developed through practice, effort, and the right conditions.”

Like any mental muscle, creativity needs exercise to develop. If you’re just learning to play guitar, you may not yet have enough musical vocabulary to improvise. Yet you can write a song after learning only three chords. All you need is an idea and a melody. It can be fun to create something original, even if it wouldn’t pass critical muster. Try making something just for the fun of it, without criticizing the outcome. Let yourself play in the sandbox of creativity. It might make you happier.

I think there should be a Family Feud game for divergent thinkers. You would try to pick the most novel answers to the questions asked, and the person who picks logical items that no one else chooses wins. Here’s a fun question to start: “What items might be found in a national ballroom?”

item.title: Can a Sleep Divorce Save Your Marriage?
item.description:
Sleep

Can a Sleep Divorce Save Your Marriage?

How sleeping apart can bring you and your spouse closer together.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Poor sleep can affect your mood, health, sex life, and how you feel about your marriage.
  • Before considering a divorce, ask yourself whether exhaustion is influencing how you view your relationship.
  • A sleep study can help uncover medical issues that may be disrupting your sleep or your partner’s.
  • If you sleep separately, make time for cuddling, sex, and meaningful conversations to connect while awake.
Sleep divorce
Source: Slaapwijsheid.nl / Unsplash

Part of being a family lawyer is knowing how to divorce a couple. Meaning, how to extricate two people from a legal union so they can stand on their own two feet as they move forward independently and, if applicable, as co-parents afterward. This is the obvious part of what I do. The other, less obvious role I have is figuring out whether someone who ends up on a call with me actually needs me for a dissolution.

I suspect I’m dealing with the latter situation when someone tells me they aren’t sleeping, they’re up all night because their partner’s waking or keeping them up, and that it’s negatively affecting their marriage in every way imaginable: they’re irritable, resentful, experiencing weight gain, and a slew of other health problems. They’re also too tired to have sex, so they’ve stopped or practically stopped. But, and this is key, they also tell me they love their spouse and the life they’ve built together and aren’t sure if they want to take such a hard approach, at least just yet.

I’m not a medical doctor, but I’ve been married twice, this time to my forever partner, so I recognize how important sleep is for quality of life and how different sleep habits can cause a host of issues if you don’t keep them in check. This is why I suggest getting to the bottom of what’s keeping you awake at night and, if need be, engaging in what’s colloquially known as a sleep divorce, where you and your partner stay married and do everything married couples typically do—except sleep in the same bed. But before going this route, here’s what I suggest doing first.

Consider Whether It’s Exhaustion That’s Affecting How You Feel About Your Marriage

According to a 2017 study, more than one-third of Americans don’t get enough sleep, and it’s taking a toll not only on people’s physical health but on their mental health as well. The researchers leading the study suggest that those who are sleep-deprived find it more challenging to be positive-minded than those who are adequately rested, and that an inability to be positive is a common symptom of depression.

Depression, another study finds, can increase the likelihood of divorce. Based on these conclusions, it might be worth considering whether your thoughts about the quality of your marriage are actually rooted in the quality of your sleep or something else.

See a Sleep Specialist for an Assessment or Suggest Your Partner Does

The most obvious way to find out whether poor sleep is the culprit in your marital woes is to actually start getting a good night’s sleep. If you’re keeping your partner up at night, or your partner is keeping you awake because of an apparent medical issue, such as snoring, it’s time to visit a specialist for a sleep study. A sleep study provides data so a medical practitioner can understand what’s going on physically during the night and address it.

If your health is being negatively affected by a partner disrupting your sleep, what’s causing them to wake you may pose a similar or even greater health risk for them. If you aren’t sleeping because your partner is simply inconsiderate, it’s time to address that as well with a conversation and some ground rules.

Come Up With Workable Solutions as a Couple

Trial and error should become your M.O. If you’re first attempting to get to the bottom of a medical mystery, it may take weeks to months to get the answers you need and, once you do, to treat the issue. In the meantime, you may want to try a few other approaches.

That may include adjusting the bedroom temperature and reducing any light coming in. It may also include the person without the medical issue heading to bed first so it’s easier for them to fall asleep, getting earplugs, or moving to a different location once they’ve been woken up. If all else fails, it may be time to try sleeping in separate rooms, aka, get a sleep divorce.

If You Opt for a Sleep Divorce

A lot can happen in the bedroom in the moments before falling asleep, and if you’re retreating to separate rooms at this time, you may want to do the following so you and your spouse don’t become further disconnected, causing a sleep divorce to become a precursor to a real divorce.

Make Time to Cuddle

Spending time together before bed, engaging in personal touch that’s not intended to lead to sex, is an important practice to maintain. Hold hands while watching TV, lay your head on your partner’s shoulder, cuddle under a blanket. If you’re comfortable visiting each other’s bedrooms and doing these things there until it’s time to actually go to sleep, try that. Communicate about what’s comfortable for both of you, then make it a habit.

Schedule Sex

If you’re finding that due to sleeping in separate bedrooms, sex isn’t happening organically, schedule it or make a point to suggest it. Given you’re not in the same bed where sex may be easier to initiate, you may have to rely on using your words more than in the past. Sleeping together less shouldn’t equate to communicating less. Even better is if it leads to communicating more. Speaking of which…

Leave Time for Pillow Talk

Whether you’re planning on having sex or not, or are basking in the afterglow, lying together in bed before falling asleep is when couples have their most intimate conversations. A sleep divorce can interfere with that if you let it. So don’t.

Not only should you make time for these conversations, but you should savor them. The more quality conversations you engage in, the closer you become. In my experience, spouses who invest time and attention into each other and their marriages tend to stay married. Where you sleep is far less consequential than what you do when you’re awake.

item.title: How to Overcome Retirement Anxiety
item.description:
Aging

How to Overcome Retirement Anxiety

Strategies to settle into a sensational, serene new chapter in the golden years.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Anticipatory stress is a response to the uncertainty of the workweek.
  • Monday anxiety raises cortisol levels and increases cardiac risk.
  • Retirees can re-program emotional responses by planning an enjoyable Monday morning.

The decision to leave the workforce is bittersweet for some and exciting for others—who have been literally counting the days, and even hours, until the jail gate swings open. But when the day comes and goes, after the retirement party is over, the anxiety remains. This phenomenon, which is unexpected for many recent retirees, lingers over time. Fortunately, it has a name, an explanation, and a solution. Research explains.

Source: Image by Mircea Iancu from Pixabay

The "Anxious Monday" Effect

Tarani Chandola et al. (2025) investigated the cause of what they term “anxious Mondays” in 3511 older adults aged 50 or older living in England.[i] They discovered a link between Monday anxiety and higher cortisol levels measured through hair samples; they did not find significant differences in cortisol levels produced by anxiety on other days of the week. Interestingly, regarding retirees, Chandola and team found that both working and nonworking older adults experience Monday anxiety, proving the phenomenon is tied to the start of the week rather than employment.

Regarding Mondays, the researchers also recognize it the day as linked with higher levels of cardiovascular disease events, with a 19 percent increase in confirmed myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac deaths, a statistic found in both men and women both above and below age 65. They also recognize the “Monday blues” effect on mood, highlighting the psychological effects of beginning the work week. Regarding cortisol levels, Chandola and colleagues explain that stress triggers the nervous system to activate a physiological process that increases cortisol levels.

Interpreting their results, Chandola and team conclude that the Monday effect reflects the reality that although most people adapt to Monday anxiety over their working life, not everyone adjusts. Some people continue to experience the effect after they retire.

Monday Uncertainty

Tarani Chandola and Benjamin Becker noted that one reason Mondays may be stressful for both working and nonworking adults is the uncertainty that accompanies the start of the workweek; another is that the Monday effect may become an automatic response and persist even after retirement, shaped through decades of routine.[ii]

Regardless of the explanation, finding a solution to Monday blues may improve quality of life both physically and emotionally. One way to address the issue is to replace the dread and uncertainty of a coming week by planning it instead.

Retirement as Planning Pleasure

Counteracting ingrained patterns of thinking and behaving in anticipation of the week's start may be easier when addressing both thoughts and behavior. Intentionally planning enjoyable activities on Monday may counteract the stress previously associated with the uncertainty and anxiety of the workweek. Here are some ideas.

Connecting with retired colleagues. Share the enjoyment of being free from workplace demands with a former co-worker in your same situation. Joining a group of retirees within your industry or area of expertise can provide a robust social life that carries forth the meaning behind your career choice, without the daily stress.

Reconnecting with faith, family, and friends. Retirement is a unique opportunity to recapture the joy of experiencing what you missed for so many years—relationships. Plan Mondays as a day to schedule coveted family time, and meet with people you haven’t seen or spoken to when you were “too busy.”

Rescheduling Monday. Counteract the ingrained emotional reaction to an unpredictable week and schedule an enjoyable Monday morning activity to replace uncertainty with pleasure; coffee with a friend, a walk on the beach with your spouse, or a road trip bucket-list adventure gives you something exciting to look forward to. Ideally designed to replace the stress and anxiety of an unpredictable week, pre-scheduling Monday will also help prevent the “Sunday blues” that often foreshadow the morning to come.

Ideally, the plan is to enjoy retirement every day of the week, as you have the luxury of planning the best years of your life.
